headline: Canopy Growth's international sales jump 141% on German demand
dek: Canopy's quarter to 30 September showed revenue up 22% to C$81.4M, while Cronos posted record German sales, a sign Europe's medical market is now driving Canadian growers.
key_points: Canopy Growth's international cannabis revenue rose 141% to C$12.3M in its fiscal second quarter, led by Germany and Poland.
Total revenue grew 22% to C$81.4M, but the net loss widened by C$35.7M on fair value charges tied to Canopy USA assets.
Cronos Group reported a day earlier that net revenue rose 75% to US$63.5M, with record sales in Germany and Israel.
Both companies are building EU GMP supply chains, the certification that lets Canadian flower enter European pharmacies.
body: Europe's medical cannabis market is now doing measurable work for Canada's largest producers. Canopy Growth said on 6 November that its international cannabis revenue rose 141% to C$12.3 million in the three months to 30 September, up from C$5.1 million a year earlier, and it named Germany and Poland as the drivers.

Cronos Group, reporting a day earlier, described a similar pull. The company said its international business outside Israel set another revenue record, led by demand in Germany, as total net revenue rose 75% to US$63.5 million. Two quarterly reports do not make a trend on their own, but they point the same way: European medical demand is lifting the Canadians who can supply it.

Canopy's consolidated net revenue rose 22% to C$81.4 million in its second quarter of fiscal 2027. The cannabis segment grew 30% to C$66.2 million. Inside that, Canadian medical sales rose 18% to C$25.8 million, which the company tied to more insured customers and its purchase of MTL Cannabis. Canadian adult-use sales rose 17% to C$28.1 million, mostly from more flower sales through MTL, partly offset by fewer opportunistic bulk deals. Storz & Bickel, its vaporizer maker, slipped 4% to C$15.1 million.

Margins went the other way. Consolidated gross margin fell to 29% from 33%. Canopy blamed the cannabis segment's decline mainly on Veterans Affairs Canada cutting its reimbursement rate for medical cannabis, which StratCann reports dropped from C$8 to C$6.50 a gram on 1 April. The net loss grew by C$35.7 million from a year earlier, which the company attributed to C$35.8 million of fair value charges on assets related to Canopy USA, its vehicle for US cannabis interests.

On the cash side the picture improved slightly. The adjusted EBITDA loss was C$2.9 million, C$0.2 million better than a year earlier, and free cash outflow shrank to C$15.5 million from C$19.2 million. Chief financial officer Tom Stewart said positive adjusted EBITDA is within reach during fiscal 2027.

Excise remains a heavy weight on Canadian adult-use sales. StratCann calculated that Canopy paid C$14.9 million in excise on C$28.1 million of net adult-use revenue, a rate of about 53%, against roughly 13% on medical sales.
> Canada is where these companies sell most; Europe is where they are growing fastest.

Canopy spent the quarter building the plumbing for exports. Its Smiths Falls, Ontario, facility gained EU Good Manufacturing Practice certification in October, which the company says makes it Canada's only EU GMP site combining softgel manufacturing with primary packaging of softgels, oral liquids and dried flower. Its Kincardine, Ontario, cultivation site had its EU GMP certification renewed by a German authority in August. It hired a country manager for Germany, entered the UK through distributor GROW Group with four flower strains under its Spectrum Therapeutics brand, and added products in Australia.

Chief executive Luc Mongeau credited strong medical sales in Germany and Poland and told analysts the company sees international markets as a key growth driver. On the call, management tied segment growth to higher flower production and supply for both Canada and Europe.
## Cronos: Israel, Germany and now the Netherlands

Cronos reports in US dollars and has a different mix. It said higher flower sales in Israel and other countries, specifically Germany, which carry no excise tax, drove the jump in revenue, along with higher flower and extract sales in Canada and a stronger Israeli shekel. Gross margin edged up to 50.9%, net income was US$17.8 million, and adjusted EBITDA rose to US$17.1 million from US$5.7 million.

Cronos also closed its acquisition of CanAdelaar in October, which it says gives it a leading position in the Netherlands, which it calls Europe's largest adult-use market. The company held about US$840 million in cash, restricted cash and interest-bearing deposits at quarter end.

The detail both companies flag is excise. Product sold into Canadian provinces carries federal and provincial duty, while medical exports to Germany and Israel do not, according to Cronos. That makes each euro of German revenue worth more at the gross-profit line than a dollar of Ontario retail revenue. The risk sits in Berlin. Germany's 2024 reforms took medical cannabis out of the Narcotics Act and let pharmacies fill telemedicine prescriptions, which opened the door to online platforms. A government bill adopted by the federal cabinet in October 2025 would require an in-person visit before a first prescription and ban mail-order sales, according to law firm Gleiss Lutz. That would hit the channel that has carried much of the new demand.

Three things. Where Germany's curbs on telemedicine prescriptions and mail-order dispensing land, which will test how durable this growth is. Whether Canopy's international line keeps growing quarter on quarter as its Kincardine site, which management told analysts could lift flower yields by 25% to 30% in the same footprint, converts more grow rooms. And whether Canopy delivers the positive adjusted EBITDA its CFO has said is within reach this fiscal year, which ends on 31 March 2027.
